content: Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib) disease is a severe illness caused by a bacterial infection. It primarily affects children under the age of 5. Your child can contract Hib disease by being in close contact with other children or adults who carry the bacteria, even if those individuals do not show symptoms. The bacteria spread from person to person. If the bacteria remain in the nose and throat, the child may not become ill. However, if the bacteria spread to the lungs or bloodstream, they can cause serious health problems. Before the introduction of the Hib vaccine, Hib disease was the leading cause of bacterial meningitis in children under 5 years old in the United States. Meningitis is an infection of the protective coverings of the brain and spinal cord, which can result in permanent brain damage and hearing loss. Hib disease can also lead to pneumonia, severe throat swelling that can obstruct breathing, infections of the blood, joints, bones, and the lining of the heart, and even death. Prior to the vaccine, approximately 20,000 children under 5 in the U.S. developed severe Hib disease annually, and nearly 1,000 of them died. The Hib vaccine is highly effective in preventing Hib disease, and discontinuing vaccination would result in a significant increase in cases. Children should receive the Hib vaccine at the following ages: 2 months, 4 months, 6 months (depending on the vaccine brand, this dose may not be necessary; your healthcare provider will advise you), and 12–15 months. If a dose is missed or delayed, the next dose should be administered as soon as possible without restarting the series. The Hib vaccine can be given alongside other vaccines. Children over 5 years old typically do not require the Hib vaccine, but certain older children and adults with specific health conditions should receive it. These conditions include sickle cell disease, HIV/AIDS, removal of the spleen, bone marrow transplant, or cancer treatment with immunosuppressive drugs. Consult your healthcare provider for more information. Individuals who have experienced a life-threatening allergic reaction to a previous dose of the Hib vaccine should not receive another dose. The vaccine is not recommended for children under 6 weeks of age. Those who are moderately or severely ill at the time of vaccination should usually wait until they recover before receiving the Hib vaccine. Consult your healthcare provider for further guidance. Like any medication, vaccines can cause side effects, including rare but serious allergic reactions. However, the risk of the Hib vaccine causing severe harm or death is extremely low. Most individuals who receive the vaccine experience no problems. Mild side effects may include redness, warmth, or swelling at the injection site (affecting up to 25% of children) and fever over 101°F (affecting up to 5% of children). These symptoms typically begin within a day of vaccination and last 2–3 days. If a moderate or severe reaction occurs, such as a serious allergic reaction, high fever, or behavioral changes, seek medical attention immediately. Signs of a severe allergic reaction may include difficulty breathing, hoarseness or wheezing, hives, paleness, weakness, rapid heartbeat, or dizziness, which can occur within minutes to hours after vaccination. If such a reaction occurs, contact a doctor immediately and provide details about the reaction, including the date and time it occurred and when the vaccine was administered. Ask your healthcare provider to file a Vaccine Adverse Event Reporting System (VAERS) form, or you can contact VAERS directly at 1-800-822-7967 or visit their website. In rare cases of serious vaccine-related injury, the National Vaccine Injury Compensation Program (VICP) provides financial assistance for medical care. For more information about the VICP, call 1-800-338-2382 or visit their website. For additional information, consult your doctor or healthcare provider. They can provide the vaccine package insert or recommend other reliable sources. You can also contact your local or state health department’s immunization program or the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) at 1-800-232-4636 (1-800-CDC-INFO) or visit the National Immunization Program’s website.
